<reason>Both sides argued competently, but A (CON) built the more durable structure. A's core move—that priority should track marginal reachable benefit rather than category—survived scrutiny because A neutralized B's two strongest weapons. On cost/equity, A exposed that B was treating gyms as sunk cost while charging digital proposals for hardware/connectivity from scratch, even though B's own opening had cited widespread Chromebook distribution; A's "compare existing assets consistently" line (A2.5, A4.2) went unanswered in B's later rounds. On the "unmet need" default, B's Rebuttal 2 answer to the override question quietly hardened into requiring physical/arts to be "fully funded and staffed with open capacity" before digital could take priority—effectively a near-unfalsifiable exception. A caught this shift explicitly (A4.3, A5.1) and B's closing never addressed it, instead reasserting the aggregate-data framing without engaging the objection that national trends don't determine which marginal expansion serves more excluded students at a given school. B's closing claim that A "conceded" B's rule is rhetorically effective but overstates what A actually said, and doesn't repair the unaddressed exception-inflation problem. B's opening being clipped is a minor execution cost. B's data-vs-hypothetical framing was vivid and nearly carried the round, but the unrebutted technical points tip it to A.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's sunk-cost symmetry argument (A2.5→A4.2), combined with catching B's exception criterion quietly hardening into "fully funded and staffed with open capacity" (A4.3/A5.1)—both left unanswered by B's closing—did the most damage to PRO's live route to victory.</best_rebuttal>
